back: 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

front: What alternative observation confirms ammonia gas is present during the ammonium ion test?
back: Ammonia gas produces **white smoke** when it comes into contact with fumes of **hydrogen chloride** (from concentrated HCl). The white smoke is **ammonium chloride**: NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + HCl (g) → NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s).

front: What are **halogens**?
back: **Halogens** are the Group 7 elements: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine. They are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules at room temperature and become progressively darker in colour going down the group.

front: What is a **halogen displacement reaction**?
back: A **halogen displacement reaction** is a reaction in which a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.

front: What is a **disproportionation reaction**?
back: A **disproportionation reaction** is a reaction in which the same species is simultaneously both oxidised and reduced.

front: Why does the reducing power of halide ions increase going down Group 7?
back: Going down the group, the halide ions become larger and have more electron **shielding**. Their outer electrons are held less tightly by the nucleus, so it is easier to lose electrons, making larger halide ions stronger **reducing agents**.

front: Define **volatility**
back: **Volatility** is how easily a substance evaporates. A more volatile substance has a lower boiling point.

front: What colour change is seen when chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution?
back: The solution turns **yellow-orange** as bromine is displaced and formed in solution. If an organic solvent is added, the organic layer also appears **yellow-orange**.

front: What type of compound is formed when a halogen reacts with a Group 1 or Group 2 metal?
back: An **ionic** compound called a **metal halide salt** is formed. In these reactions the metal is always **oxidised** and the halogen acts as the **oxidising agent**.

front: What is observed when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium chloride?
back: **Misty fumes** of hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas are produced. No further reaction occurs because Cl<sup>-</sup> is a weak reducing agent and cannot reduce the sulfuric acid further.

front: Why do the boiling points of the halogens increase going down Group 7?
back: Going down the group, the halogen molecules have more electrons, so **London dispersion forces** between molecules become stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point increases.

front: What colour change is seen when chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
back: The solution turns **brown** as iodine is displaced. If an organic solvent such as cyclohexane is added, the organic layer appears **purple**.

front: What oxidation state does iron reach when it reacts with chlorine or bromine?
back: Iron is oxidised from Fe<sup>2+</sup> to **Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup>. Both chlorine and bromine are strong enough **oxidising agents** to bring about this change.

front: When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium bromide, a **..........**  gas is first formed, which is then oxidised to give a **..........**  gas of bromine.
back: When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium bromide, a **hydrogen bromide** gas is first formed, which is then oxidised to give a **reddish-brown** gas of bromine.

front: The halogens are held together by **..........**. These forces get stronger as the number of **..........**  in the molecule increases going down the group.
back: The halogens are held together by **London dispersion forces**. These forces get stronger as the number of **electrons** in the molecule increases going down the group.

front: When bromine solution is added to potassium iodide solution, the solution turns **..........**. If an organic solvent is added, the organic layer turns **..........** as iodine is formed.
back: When bromine solution is added to potassium iodide solution, the solution turns **brown**. If an organic solvent is added, the organic layer turns **purple** as iodine is formed.

front:
**True or False?**

Iodine can oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions.
back:
**False.**

Iodine is not a strong enough **oxidising agent** to oxidise Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>. In fact, iron(III) ions oxidise **iodide ions** to iodine, not the other way around.

front: What observations are made when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium iodide?
back:
1. Misty fumes of **HI** gas are seen.
2. A **purple** vapour of I<sub>2</sub> and choking **SO**<sub>**2**</sub> gas are produced.
3. A **yellow** solid of sulfur appears.
4. A **bad egg** smell of H<sub>2</sub>S gas is detected.

front: What is the trend in electronegativity going down Group 7?
back: **Electronegativity decreases** going down the group. Larger atoms have a greater atomic radius and more electron shielding, so the nucleus attracts bonding electrons less strongly.

front: Why is an organic solvent useful in halogen displacement reactions?
back: Halogens are more **soluble** in the organic layer than in the aqueous layer. This makes the colour changes easier to observe, helping to identify which halogen has been produced.

front: In the reaction of iodide ions with iron(III), iodide is **..........**  and iron(III) is **..........**.
back: In the reaction of iodide ions with iron(III), iodide is **oxidised** and iron(III) is **reduced**.

front: What colours are the precipitates formed by Cl<sup>-</sup>, Br<sup>-</sup>, and I<sup>-</sup> with silver nitrate?
back: AgCl is **white**. AgBr is **cream**. AgI is **pale yellow**. The precipitates are formed by adding silver nitrate solution to the unknown halide solution acidified with nitric acid.

front: Define **electronegativity**
back: **Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to attract electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

front: In the displacement of bromine by chlorine, which species is oxidised and which is reduced?
back: **Bromine** is oxidised: Br goes from -1 to 0. **Chlorine** is reduced: Cl goes from 0 to -1. The reaction is therefore a **redox** reaction.

front: What products are formed when chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH (around 15°C)?
back: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH to form **NaCl** and **NaClO** (sodium chlorate(I)). This is a **disproportionation** reaction: chlorine is reduced to Cl<sup>-</sup> (ox. no. 0 to −1) and oxidised to ClO<sup>-</sup> (ox. no. 0 to +1).

front: Silver chloride dissolves in **..........**  ammonia. Silver bromide only dissolves in **..........**  ammonia. Silver iodide is insoluble in both.
back: Silver chloride dissolves in **dilute** ammonia. Silver bromide only dissolves in **concentrated** ammonia. Silver iodide is insoluble in both.

front:
**True or False?**

Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
back:
**True.**

Fluorine is the smallest halogen with the least electron shielding. Its nucleus attracts incoming electrons most strongly, making it the most powerful **oxidising agent** and the most reactive halogen.

front: A more reactive halogen can **..........**  a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide ions because more reactive halogens are stronger **..........**.
back: A more reactive halogen can **displace** a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide ions because more reactive halogens are stronger **oxidising agents**.

front: What products are formed when chlorine reacts with hot concentrated NaOH (around 70°C)?
back: Chlorine reacts with hot NaOH to form **NaCl** and **NaClO**<sub>**3**</sub> (sodium chlorate(V)). Chlorine is oxidised to ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (ox. no. 0 to +5) and reduced to Cl<sup>-</sup> (ox. no. 0 to −1).

front:
**True or False?**

Silver iodide dissolves in concentrated ammonia solution.
back:
**False.**

**Silver iodide** does not dissolve in either dilute or concentrated ammonia. This distinguishes iodide from chloride and bromide in the **silver nitrate test**.

front: Why does the oxidising power of halogens decrease down Group 7?
back: Going down the group, atomic radius increases and there is more electron **shielding**. Incoming electrons are attracted less strongly by the nucleus, so each halogen is less able to gain an electron and act as an **oxidising agent**.

front:
**True or False?**

Bromine can displace chloride ions from potassium chloride solution.
back:
**False.**

Bromine is less reactive than chlorine. Only a **more reactive** halogen can displace a less reactive one. Bromine can only displace iodide ions, not chloride ions.

front: The reaction of chlorine with water is a **..........**  reaction in which chlorine is reduced to HCl and oxidised to **..........** acid.
back: The reaction of chlorine with water is a **disproportionation** reaction in which chlorine is reduced to HCl and oxidised to **chloric(I)** acid.

front: What is produced when a hydrogen halide gas reacts with ammonia gas?
back: An **ammonium halide** salt is formed as a solid. For example, HCl (g) + NH<sub>3</sub> (g) → NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s).

front: Going down Group 7, the reaction of the halogens with hydrogen gas becomes less **..........**.
back: Going down Group 7, the reaction of the halogens with hydrogen gas becomes less **vigorous**.

front: Write the ionic equation for the displacement of iodide ions by bromine.
back:
Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → 2Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) + I<sub>2</sub> (aq)

Iodide ions are **oxidised** (−1 to 0) and bromine is **reduced** (0 to −1).

front: How does chlorine make drinking water safe?
back: Chlorine reacts with water to form **chloric(I) acid** (HClO), which kills **bacteria** and acts as a sterilising agent. HClO can also dissociate to form ClO<sup>-</sup>, which is also a sterilising agent.

front: Why must reactions of halide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid be carried out in a fume cupboard?
back: The reactions produce **toxic gases** such as HCl, HBr, SO<sub>2</sub>, and H<sub>2</sub>S. A fume cupboard prevents these harmful gases from escaping into the laboratory.

front: Why can silver nitrate not be used to test for fluoride ions?
back: **Silver fluoride** (AgF) is **soluble** in water, so no precipitate forms. This is an exception to the general trend for silver halides, which are insoluble.

front: Define **activation energy**
back: The **activation energy** (*E*<sub>a</sub>) is the minimum energy that reacting particles must possess for a collision to result in a chemical reaction.

front: What is a **successful collision**?
back: A **successful collision** (also called an effective collision) is one in which the particles collide with the correct **orientation** and with energy equal to or greater than the **activation energy**, resulting in a chemical reaction.

front: What is **collision frequency** and what factors affect it?
back: **Collision frequency** is the number of collisions between particles per unit time. It is increased by raising **concentration**, **pressure**, **temperature**, or increasing the **surface area** of solid reactants.

front: For a collision to be effective, particles must collide in the correct **..........**  and with energy at least equal to the **..........** of the reaction.
back: For a collision to be effective, particles must collide in the correct **orientation** and with energy at least equal to the **activation energy** of the reaction.

front: Why does increasing concentration increase the rate of reaction?
back: A higher **concentration** means more particles are present in the same volume. This leads to more frequent **collisions** and therefore more successful collisions per unit time.

front:
**True or False?**

In an endothermic reaction, the activation energy is smaller than in an exothermic reaction.
back:
**False.**

In an **endothermic** reaction, the products are higher in energy than the reactants, so the energy barrier is larger. The **activation energy** in endothermic reactions is relatively larger than in exothermic reactions.

front: What is an unsuccessful collision between reactant particles?
back: An **unsuccessful collision** is one where particles either collide in the wrong **orientation** or lack sufficient energy to reach the **activation energy**. The particles bounce off each other and no reaction occurs.

front: In an exothermic reaction, the reactants are **..........**  in energy than the products, so the activation energy is relatively **..........** compared to an endothermic reaction.
back: In an exothermic reaction, the reactants are **higher** in energy than the products, so the activation energy is relatively **smaller** compared to an endothermic reaction.

front: Give three ways to measure the rate of a chemical reaction.
back:
1. Measure the amount of **reactant** lost over time.
2. Measure the amount of **product** formed over time.
3. Measure the time taken for a colour change or a set amount of **precipitate** to form.

front: Define **rate of reaction**
back: The **rate of reaction** is the speed at which a chemical reaction takes place. It is measured in mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> and equals the change in concentration of a reactant or product divided by time.

front: How is the instantaneous rate of reaction found from a concentration–time graph?
back: A **tangent** is drawn to the curve at the point of interest. The **gradient** of the tangent (Δy ÷ Δx) gives the instantaneous rate of reaction at that time.

front: Rate of reaction = change in amount of **..........**  or products divided by **..........** .
back: Rate of reaction = change in amount of **reactants** or products divided by **time**.

front: As a reaction proceeds, the concentration of reactants **..........**  and the concentration of products **..........** .
back: As a reaction proceeds, the concentration of reactants **decreases** and the concentration of products **increases**.

front: What is the main limitation of measuring reaction rate by mass loss when a gas is produced?
back: The gas must be sufficiently **dense** for the mass change to be detectable on a balance. Light gases such as hydrogen (Mr = 2.0) cause too small a mass change to measure accurately.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrogen gas is suitable for the mass loss method of measuring reaction rate.
back:
**False.**

**Hydrogen** has a very low *M*<sub>r</sub> (2.0), so the mass loss is too small to detect on a balance. Only gases with a sufficiently high *M*<sub>r</sub>, such as CO<sub>2</sub> (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 44.0), are suitable.

front: What is the disappearing cross experiment and what does it measure?
back: Sodium thiosulfate reacts with HCl to produce a **yellow** precipitate of sulfur. A cross beneath the flask is timed until it can no longer be seen through the solution, giving a measure of **reaction rate**.

front: What is **quenching** in the context of measuring reaction rates?
back: **Quenching** is the deliberate stopping of a reaction at a specific time so that a sample can be taken and analysed by **titration** without the reaction continuing during the analysis.

front: What does a graph of gas volume against time show about the rate of reaction?
back: The **gradient** of the graph at any point shows the rate of reaction at that time. The gradient decreases over time as the reactant **concentration** falls and the reaction slows.

front: What is a **Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve**?
back: A **Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve** is a graph showing the distribution of kinetic energies among the particles in a gas sample at a given temperature.

front: What does the activation energy marker on a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve show?
back: The **activation energy** (*E*<sub>a</sub>) marker divides the curve into two regions. Only particles with energy equal to or greater than *E*<sub>a</sub> can undergo **successful collisions** and react.

front: In a sample of gas at a given temperature, a few particles have very **..........**  energy, a few have very **..........**  energy, and most have energy in between.
back: In a sample of gas at a given temperature, a few particles have very **low** energy, a few have very **high** energy, and most have energy in between.

front: How does the shape of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve change when temperature increases?
back: The curve **flattens** and the peak shifts to the **right**. This means a greater proportion of particles have energies above the **activation energy**.

front:
**True or False?**

At higher temperature, the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shifts to the left.
back:
**False.**

At higher temperature, the peak shifts to the **right** and the curve **flattens**. This reflects the higher average kinetic energy of the particles.

front: Give two reasons why increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction.
back:
1. Particles move faster, leading to more **frequent collisions**.
2. A greater **proportion** of particles have kinetic energy equal to or greater than the **activation energy**, so more collisions are successful.

front: At higher temperatures, the proportion of particles with energy greater than the activation energy **..........**,  so the rate of reaction **..........** .
back: At higher temperatures, the proportion of particles with energy greater than the activation energy **increases**, so the rate of reaction **increases**.

front: Why does the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve never touch the x-axis at high energies?
back: There is always a small number of particles with very high **kinetic energy**. The curve approaches but never reaches zero, reflecting the **statistical distribution** of energies in the sample.

front: Define **catalyst**
back: A **catalyst** is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower **activation energy**. It is not consumed in the reaction.

front: What is a **homogeneous catalyst**?
back: A **homogeneous catalyst** is one that is in the same **phase** as the reactants, for example when both the catalyst and reactants are dissolved in solution.

front: What is a **heterogeneous catalyst**?
back: A **heterogeneous catalyst** is one that is in a different **phase** from the reactants, for example a solid catalyst used with gaseous reactants. This is the most common type in industry.

front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
back: A **catalyst** provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower **activation energy**. A greater proportion of particles now have energy equal to or above *E*<sub>a</sub>, so more collisions are successful.

front:
**True or False?**

A heterogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants.
back:
**False.**

A **heterogeneous** catalyst is in a **different phase** from the reactants. For example, the catalyst may be a solid while the reactants are gases.

front: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, a catalyst shifts the **..........**  to a lower value, so a greater proportion of particles have energy above the **..........** .
back: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, a catalyst shifts the **activation energy** to a lower value, so a greater proportion of particles have energy above the **activation energy**.

front: Give three advantages of using catalysts in chemical reactions.
back:
1. They increase the **rate of reaction**, so more product is made in a given time.
2. They reduce **energy costs** as the reaction can occur at lower temperatures and pressures.
3. They can increase **atom economy** by reducing unwanted side reactions.

front: Why does a catalyst increase the proportion of successful collisions?
back: A catalyst lowers the **activation energy** by providing an alternative pathway. More particles in the sample have energies exceeding this lower *E*<sub>a</sub>, leading to more **effective collisions** per unit time.

front: A **..........**  catalyst is the most common type in industry, where the catalyst is in a **..........**  phase from the reactants.
back: A **heterogeneous** catalyst is the most common type in industry, where the catalyst is in a **different** phase from the reactants.

front: What is a **reversible reaction**?
back: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the products can react to reform the original reactants. It is represented using two opposing half-arrows (⇌).

front: Define **dynamic equilibrium**
back: **Dynamic equilibrium** exists in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of all reactants and products remain **constant**.

front: What is a **closed system**?
back: A **closed system** is one in which none of the reactants or products can escape from the reaction mixture. Dynamic equilibrium can only be established in a closed system.

front: What two conditions are required for a dynamic equilibrium to exist?
back:
1. The reaction must occur in a **closed system**.
2. The rate of the **forward** reaction must equal the rate of the **backward** reaction.

front:
**True or False?**

At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
back:
**False.**

At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are **constant**, not equal. The actual concentrations of each species can be very different from one another.

front: At dynamic equilibrium, the rate of the **..........**  reaction equals the rate of the **..........**  reaction.
back: At dynamic equilibrium, the rate of the **forward** reaction equals the rate of the **backward** reaction.

front: Why can reactions involving gases only reach equilibrium in a closed system?
back: In an **open system**, gases can escape to the surroundings. This prevents the backward reaction from occurring and causes the reaction to go to **completion** rather than reaching equilibrium.

front:
**True or False?**

In a dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions have stopped.
back:
**False.**

In a **dynamic equilibrium**, both the forward and backward reactions continue at the same rate. The term "dynamic" reflects that the particles are constantly reacting.

front: What is the difference between an open and a closed system?
back: In a **closed system**, no reactants or products can escape the reaction mixture. In an **open system**, matter and energy can be lost to the surroundings, preventing equilibrium from being established.

front: What is **Le Chatelier's principle**?
back: **Le Chatelier's principle** states that if a change is made to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract that change.

front: What is the **position of equilibrium**?
back: The **position of equilibrium** refers to the relative amounts of reactants and products in an equilibrium mixture. It can shift left (towards reactants) or right (towards products).

front: What happens to the equilibrium position when the concentration of a reactant is increased?
back: The equilibrium shifts to the **right** to use up the excess reactant. This increases the concentration of **products** and restores balance.

front: Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **..........**  moles of gas. Decreasing pressure shifts it towards the side with **..........**  moles of gas.
back: Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **fewer** moles of gas. Decreasing pressure shifts it towards the side with **more** moles of gas.

front: What effect does changing the pressure have on an equilibrium where both sides have equal moles of gas?
back: There is **no effect** on the equilibrium position. The shift in equilibrium caused by a pressure change only occurs when there are different numbers of moles of **gas** on each side.

front:
**True or False?**

Increasing temperature always shifts the equilibrium towards the exothermic direction.
back:
**False.**

Increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the **endothermic** direction. The system absorbs the extra heat energy to oppose the change.

front: How does increasing temperature affect the position of an exothermic equilibrium?
back: The equilibrium shifts to the **left** (towards reactants). The system opposes the temperature increase by absorbing energy, which means the **endothermic** (reverse) reaction is favoured.

front: When the concentration of a product is decreased, the equilibrium shifts to the **..........**  to **..........**  the lost product.
back: When the concentration of a product is decreased, the equilibrium shifts to the **right** to **replace** the lost product.

front: Why does removing a product as it forms increase the yield of a reaction?
back: Removing a product decreases its **concentration**. By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts to the **right** to replace it, consuming more reactants and producing more product overall.

front: What effect does increasing pressure have when there are more moles of gas on the left side of an equation?
back: The equilibrium shifts to the **left** towards the side with fewer moles of gas. This reduces the pressure and opposes the change, in line with **Le Chatelier's principle**.

front: What is the **yield-rate compromise** in industrial chemistry?
back: The **yield-rate compromise** is the balance between choosing conditions that give a high yield and conditions that give an acceptable rate of reaction. Conditions that maximise yield often reduce rate, and vice versa.

front: Why is a temperature of approximately 450°C used in the Haber Process?
back: 450°C gives an acceptable **yield** of around 35% ammonia and an acceptable **rate** of reaction. Lower temperatures give a higher yield but the rate is too slow; higher temperatures give a faster rate but greatly reduce the yield.

front: Why are higher temperatures not used in the Haber Process to increase the rate?
back: The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the **left**, reducing the yield of ammonia. The higher energy costs also make it less economical.

front:
**True or False?**

Increasing pressure in the Haber Process decreases the yield of ammonia.
back:
**False.**

Increasing pressure **increases** the yield because there are 4 moles of gas on the reactant side but only 2 moles on the product side. The equilibrium shifts to the **right** towards fewer moles of gas.

front: In the Haber Process, there are **..........**  moles of gas on the reactant side and **..........**  moles on the product side, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right.
back: In the Haber Process, there are **4** moles of gas on the reactant side and **2** moles on the product side, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right.

front: Why is approximately 200 atm rather than 400 atm used in the Haber Process?
back: Doubling the pressure to around 400 atm only increases the yield by around **7%**, but greatly increases the **financial** and **energy costs**, and raises significant **health and safety** concerns.

front: Give three types of consideration that affect the choice of industrial reaction conditions.
back:
1. **Financial**: is the cost of altered conditions balanced by sufficient increase in profit?
2. **Energy and environmental**: will conditions increase fossil fuel use or energy costs?
3. **Health and safety**: are the proposed conditions safe for workers and equipment?

front: In the Haber Process, the temperature compromise of approximately 450°C gives a yield of around **..........** % ammonia.
back: In the Haber Process, the temperature compromise of approximately 450°C gives a yield of around **35** % ammonia.

front: Why are lower temperatures not used in the Haber Process despite giving a higher yield?
back: At lower temperatures, the **rate** of reaction is too slow. Although the equilibrium yield would be higher, the time taken to produce a commercially useful quantity of ammonia would be too long.

front: Define **addition reaction**
back:
**Addition reaction** is one in which two reactants combine to form a single product.

It is most commonly seen with alkenes, where the C=C double bond reacts with a small molecule such as H<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>O.

front: In organic chemistry, how is **oxidation** defined in terms of hydrogen and oxygen?
back:
**Oxidation** involves the loss of hydrogen or the gain of oxygen.

For example, an aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylic acid: CH<sub>3</sub>CHO + [O] → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH.

front: Define **elimination reaction**
back:
An **elimination reaction** is one in which a small molecule is removed from a reactant, forming an alkene as one of the products.

For example, a halogenoalkane can lose HBr to form an alkene.

front: In organic chemistry, how is **reduction** defined in terms of hydrogen and oxygen?
back:
**Reduction** involves the gain of hydrogen or the loss of oxygen.

For example, an aldehyde is reduced to an alcohol: CH<sub>3</sub>CHO + [H] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

front: Define **substitution reaction**
back:
A **substitution reaction** is one in which an atom or group of atoms in a compound is replaced by another atom or group of atoms.

For example, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + OH<sup>-</sup> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + Br<sup>-</sup>

front: In an **addition polymerisation** reaction, the **..........**-**..........**  double bond of an alkene monomer breaks open and forms a long **..........**  chain.
back: In an **addition polymerisation** reaction, the **carbon**-**carbon** double bond of an alkene monomer breaks open and forms a long **polymer** chain.

front: Define **hydrolysis reaction**
back:
A **hydrolysis reaction** is one in which a compound reacts with water, splitting the compound into smaller molecules.

For example, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>OH + HCl.

front:
**True or False?**

An elimination reaction always produces exactly one product.
back:
**False.**

An elimination reaction typically produces more than one product. For example, a halogenoalkane reacting with OH<sup>-</sup> under heat produces an alkene, water and a halide ion.

front: Name the **seven types of organic reaction** covered at AS level.
back:
1. **Addition**
2. **Elimination**
3. **Substitution**
4. **Oxidation**
5. **Reduction**
6. **Hydrolysis**
7. **Polymerisation**

front: Define **curly arrow** (in reaction mechanisms)
back:
A **curly arrow** is a symbol used in reaction mechanisms to show the movement of electrons.

Double-headed curly arrows show the movement of an electron pair. Single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows show the movement of a single electron.

front:
**True or False?**

Single-headed curly arrows show the movement of an electron pair.
back:
**False.**

Single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows show the movement of a **single electron**. Double-headed curly arrows show the movement of an **electron pair**.

front: Define **homolytic fission**
back:
**Homolytic fission** is the breaking of a covalent bond in which one electron goes to each atom, forming two radicals.

It is shown using single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows.

front: In the reaction C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl, the bonds are non-polar or only slightly polar, suggesting **..........**  fission and a mechanism of **free radical** **..........** .
back: In the reaction C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl, the bonds are non-polar or only slightly polar, suggesting **homolytic** fission and a mechanism of **free radical** **substitution**.

front: Define **heterolytic fission**
back:
**Heterolytic fission** is the breaking of a covalent bond in which both electrons go to one atom, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.

It is shown using double-headed curly arrows.

front: How does **bond polarity** help predict the reaction mechanism when ethene reacts with HBr?
back:
HBr contains a **polar** bond, suggesting **heterolytic** fission and a mechanism involving electrophiles or nucleophiles.

The C=C double bond of ethene attracts electrophiles, so the mechanism is most likely **electrophilic addition**.

front: Define **electrophile**
back:
An **electrophile** is an electron-deficient species that accepts a pair of electrons to form a new covalent bond.

Electrophiles are produced when heterolytic fission forms a positive ion.

front: Name the **three reaction types** in which curly arrows are used to show electron movement.
back:
1. **Addition**
2. **Substitution**
3. **Elimination**

front: Define **nucleophile**
back:
A **nucleophile** is an electron-rich species that donates a lone pair of electrons to form a new covalent bond.

Nucleophiles attack positive or δ+ centres in a molecule.

front: What are **halogenoalkanes**?
back:
**Halogenoalkanes** are organic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms in an alkane have been replaced by a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br or I).

They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the carbon bearing the halogen.

front: What **prefixes** are used when naming halogenoalkanes to indicate each halogen?
back:
1. Fluorine — **fluoro**
2. Chlorine — **chloro**
3. Bromine — **bromo**
4. Iodine — **iodo**

front: Define **primary halogenoalkane**
back:
A **primary halogenoalkane** is one in which the halogen is attached to a carbon that is bonded to only one other alkyl group.

For example, 1-bromopropane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br) is a primary halogenoalkane.

front: Define **secondary halogenoalkane**
back:
A **secondary halogenoalkane** is one in which the halogen is attached to a carbon that is bonded to two other alkyl groups.

For example, 2-bromopropane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Br)CH<sub>3</sub>) is a secondary halogenoalkane.

front: Define **tertiary halogenoalkane**
back: A **tertiary halogenoalkane** is one in which the halogen is attached to a carbon that is bonded to three other alkyl groups.

front: The compound CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Cl)CH<sub>2</sub>Br is named **..........** -bromo- **..........** -chloropropane because substituents are listed **..........** .
back: The compound CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Cl)CH<sub>2</sub>Br is named **1**-bromo-**2**-chloropropane because substituents are listed **alphabetically**.

front:
**True or False?**

When naming a halogenoalkane with two different halogens, the substituents are listed in order of increasing atomic number.
back:
**False.**

Substituents in halogenoalkane names are listed in **alphabetical** order, not by atomic number. For example, bromo is listed before chloro even though bromine has a higher atomic number.

front: How do you determine whether a halogenoalkane is **primary**, **secondary** or **tertiary**?
back:
Count the number of **alkyl groups** attached to the carbon bearing the halogen.

One alkyl group = primary. Two alkyl groups = secondary. Three alkyl groups = tertiary.

front: What nucleophile and conditions are used to convert a halogenoalkane into an **alcohol**?
back:
The nucleophile is the **hydroxide ion** (OH<sup>-</sup>).

The halogenoalkane is warmed with an **aqueous** solution of NaOH or KOH, using a small amount of ethanol as a co-solvent.

front: Why do **aqueous** NaOH and **ethanolic** NaOH give different products when reacting with a halogenoalkane?
back:
Aqueous NaOH causes **nucleophilic substitution**, producing an alcohol.

Ethanolic NaOH causes **elimination**, producing an alkene because the solvent favours the elimination pathway.

front: When bromoethane reacts with ethanolic KCN under reflux, the product is **..........**  and the carbon chain length **..........**  by one.
back: When bromoethane reacts with ethanolic KCN under reflux, the product is **propanenitrile** and the carbon chain length **increases** by one.

front: What is the product called when a halogenoalkane reacts with KCN?
back:
The product is a **nitrile**.

The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) acts as the nucleophile and replaces the halogen, extending the carbon chain by one carbon atom.

front: What are the conditions for forming a **primary amine** from a halogenoalkane?
back:
The halogenoalkane is heated under pressure with an **excess** of ethanolic ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub> dissolved in ethanol).

Excess ammonia is used to prevent further substitution of the amine product.

front:
**True or False?**

Fluoroalkanes react the fastest in nucleophilic substitution reactions with aqueous NaOH.
back:
**False.**

**Fluoroalkanes do not react at all** because the C-F bond has the highest bond enthalpy. **Iodoalkanes** react the fastest because the C-I bond is the weakest.

front: Which halogenoalkane reacts fastest with aqueous NaOH in nucleophilic substitution?
back: **Fluoroalkanes do not react at all** because the C-F bond has the highest bond enthalpy. **Iodoalkanes** react the fastest because the C-I bond is the weakest.

front: Why is **OH**<sup>**-**</sup> a better nucleophile than water when reacting with halogenoalkanes?
back:
OH<sup>-</sup> carries a **full negative charge**, making it more electron-rich and a stronger nucleophile.

In water, the oxygen only carries a **partial negative charge** (δ-), so the reaction is much slower.

front: What organic product forms when a halogenoalkane is heated with **ethanolic sodium hydroxide**?
back:
An **alkene** is formed via an elimination reaction.

The C-X bond breaks heterolytically, expelling a halide ion (X<sup>-</sup>) and forming a C=C double bond.

front: Define **nucleophilic substitution**
back: A **nucleophilic substitution** is a reaction in which a nucleophile attacks a carbon atom carrying a partial positive charge and replaces an atom or group carrying a partial negative charge.

front: Why do **halogenoalkanes** undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions?
back:
The **C-X bond is polar** because of the large difference in electronegativity between carbon and the halogen.

This gives the carbon atom a partial positive charge (δ+), making it susceptible to attack by a nucleophile.

front: Describe the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution when bromoethane reacts with aqueous OH<sup>-</sup>.
back:
The OH<sup>-</sup> ion donates a lone pair to the **δ+ carbon** of the C-Br bond, forming a new C-O bond.

Simultaneously, the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically and the bromide ion (Br<sup>-</sup>) is expelled as a leaving group, producing ethanol.

front: In the C-X bond of a halogenoalkane, the carbon carries a partial **..........**  charge and the halogen carries a partial **..........**  charge, because halogens are more **..........**  than carbon.
back: In the C-X bond of a halogenoalkane, the carbon carries a partial **positive** charge and the halogen carries a partial **negative** charge, because halogens are more **electronegative** than carbon.

front: Describe the **two steps** in the reaction of chloromethane with excess ammonia to form methylamine.
back:
Step 1: NH<sub>3</sub> attacks the **δ+ carbon** of CH<sub>3</sub>Cl by **nucleophilic substitution**, forming [CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup>.

Step 2: A second NH<sub>3</sub> molecule acts as a **base**, removing a proton from [CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup> to give methylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup>.

front:
**True or False?**

In nucleophilic substitution, the nucleophile attacks the carbon atom that carries a partial negative charge.
back:
**False.**

The nucleophile attacks the carbon atom that carries a **partial positive charge** (δ+). The atom carrying the partial negative charge is the one that is replaced (e.g. the halogen).

front: What does a curly arrow represent in a nucleophilic substitution mechanism?
back:
A curly arrow shows the movement of an **electron pair**.

A double-headed curly arrow is drawn from the lone pair of the nucleophile to the δ+ carbon, and from the C-X bond to the leaving halogen atom.

front: Why must excess ammonia be used when forming a **primary amine** from a halogenoalkane?
back:
The primary amine product is itself a nucleophile and can undergo further substitution reactions with the halogenoalkane.

Using **excess ammonia** favours the formation of the primary amine over further substituted products.

front: Describe the experimental method used to **compare the rate of hydrolysis** of different halogenoalkanes.
back:
Three test tubes are set up in a **50°C water bath**, each containing ethanol and **acidified silver nitrate** solution.

A few drops of a chloroalkane, bromoalkane and iodoalkane are added to separate test tubes and a stopwatch is started. The time for each **precipitate** to form is recorded.

front: Why is **no precipitate** formed when a fluoroalkane is used in the silver nitrate hydrolysis test?
back:
Silver fluoride is **soluble**, so no precipitate forms even if fluoride ions are produced.

This also confirms that fluoroalkanes are the least reactive halogenoalkanes and do not undergo significant hydrolysis.

front:
**True or False?**

Chloroalkanes hydrolyse the fastest because the C-Cl bond is the weakest C-X bond.
back:
**False.**

Chloroalkanes hydrolyse the **slowest** among reactive halogenoalkanes. The C-Cl bond has the **highest bond enthalpy**, making it the hardest to break.

front: State the order of reactivity of halogenoalkanes in hydrolysis, from **fastest to slowest**.
back:
**Iodoalkanes** > bromoalkanes > chloroalkanes.

Fluoroalkanes do not react at all. The weaker the **C-X bond** (lower bond enthalpy), the faster the halide ion is released and the faster the hydrolysis.

front: Why does the **C-I bond** break most easily in nucleophilic substitution?
back:
The C-I bond has the **lowest bond enthalpy** of all C-X bonds, so it requires the least energy to break.

This means iodide ions are released fastest, producing the yellow silver iodide precipitate most quickly in the silver nitrate test.

front: In the silver nitrate hydrolysis test, the **..........**  precipitate forms fastest and the **..........**  precipitate forms slowest, showing that **..........**  alkanes are the most reactive.
back: In the silver nitrate hydrolysis test, the **yellow** precipitate forms fastest and the **white** precipitate forms slowest, showing that **iodo** alkanes are the most reactive.

front: In a hydrolysis comparison between 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, which reacts the **fastest** and which the **slowest**?
back:
2-chloro-2-methylpropane (the **tertiary** halogenoalkane) reacts the fastest.

1-chlorobutane (the **primary** halogenoalkane) reacts the slowest.

front: Why is **ethanol** included in the silver nitrate hydrolysis test mixture?
back:
Ethanol acts as a **co-solvent** to help dissolve the halogenoalkane, which is not miscible with water alone.

This ensures the halogenoalkane mixes with the aqueous silver nitrate so the hydrolysis reaction can occur.

front: Why is the **C-X bond** in a halogenoalkane polar?
back:
There is a large difference in **electronegativity** between the halogen and the carbon atom.

The halogen is more electronegative, giving it a δ- charge and leaving the carbon with a δ+ charge.

front: Define **bond enthalpy**
back:
**Bond enthalpy** is the energy required to break one mole of a covalent bond in the gaseous state, averaged across similar chemical environments.

A higher bond enthalpy means the bond is stronger and harder to break.

front: State the order of **C-X bond enthalpies** from weakest to strongest across the halogenoalkanes.
back:
C-I < C-Br < C-Cl < C-F.

The **C-I bond** is the weakest and easiest to break, making **iodoalkanes** the most reactive. The C-F bond is the strongest, making fluoroalkanes the least reactive.

front: Why do different halogenoalkanes have **different rates** of substitution reactions?
back:
The rate depends on the **bond enthalpy** of the C-X bond.

Weaker C-X bonds (lower bond enthalpy) break more easily, allowing the nucleophile to replace the halogen faster. The C-I bond is weakest, so iodoalkanes react fastest.

front:
**True or False?**

Based on bond polarity alone, fluoroalkanes would be predicted to be the most reactive halogenoalkanes.
back:
**True.**

Electronegativity decreases down Group 17, so the C-F bond is the most polar, which would suggest it is most reactive. However, **bond enthalpy** is a greater factor, and the C-F bond is the strongest, so fluoroalkanes are actually the least reactive.

front: Why are **fluoroalkanes** the least reactive halogenoalkanes despite having the most polar C-X bond?
back:
The C-F bond has the **highest bond enthalpy** of all C-X bonds, making it very difficult to break.

Bond enthalpy is a greater factor than bond polarity in determining reactivity, so fluoroalkanes rarely undergo substitution reactions.

front: In substitution reactions of halogenoalkanes, the C-X bond undergoes **..........**  fission. The **..........**  alkane reacts fastest because its C-X bond has the **..........**  bond enthalpy.
back: In substitution reactions of halogenoalkanes, the C-X bond undergoes **heterolytic** fission. The **iodo** alkane reacts fastest because its C-X bond has the **lowest** bond enthalpy.

front: In the reaction CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>I + OH<sup>-</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + I<sup>-</sup>, why does the **C-I bond** break rather than a C-H bond?
back:
The C-I bond is **polar** (δ+ on carbon, δ- on iodine), making the carbon susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

The C-I bond also has a lower bond enthalpy than C-H bonds, so it is easier to break during the substitution reaction.

front: Define **alcohol**
back:
An **alcohol** is an organic compound containing a **hydroxyl** functional group (-OH).

The general formula is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>OH and alcohols are named using the suffix -ol.

front: What is the **general formula** for alcohols?
back:
The general formula for alcohols is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>OH.

For example, **methanol** is CH<sub>3</sub>OH (n = 1) and **ethanol** is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (n = 2).

front: Define **diol**
back: A **diol** is an alcohol that contains **two hydroxyl** (-OH) groups within the same molecule.

front:
**True or False?**

Ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is classified as a primary alcohol.
back:
True.

In ethanol, the carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is attached to only **one** other carbon atom (the CH<sub>3</sub> group), which is the definition of a **primary alcohol**.

front: Define **primary alcohol**
back:
A **primary alcohol** is one in which the carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is attached to only one other carbon atom (or alkyl group).

For example, ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is a primary alcohol.

front: Define **secondary alcohol**
back:
A **secondary alcohol** is one in which the carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is attached to two other carbon atoms (or alkyl groups).

For example, propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol.

front: Alcohols are named by taking the parent **..........**  name and replacing the final **e** with the suffix **.........** .
back: Alcohols are named by taking the parent **alkane** name and replacing the final **e** with the suffix **-ol**.

front: Define **tertiary alcohol**
back: A **tertiary alcohol** is one in which the carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is attached to three other carbon atoms (or alkyl groups).

front: What are the products of the **complete combustion** of an alcohol?
back:
Complete combustion of an alcohol produces **carbon dioxide** and **water**.

For example: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

front: What are the organic and inorganic products when an alcohol reacts with **PCl**<sub>**5**</sub>?
back:
The organic product is a **chloroalkane**.

The inorganic products are **phosphoryl chloride** (POCl<sub>3</sub>) and **hydrogen chloride** (HCl gas). For example: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + PCl<sub>5</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl.

front: The dehydration of ethanol using concentrated phosphoric acid produces **..........**  and **..........**  as products.
back: The dehydration of ethanol using concentrated phosphoric acid produces **ethene** and **water** as products.

front: How can **PCl**<sub>**5**</sub> be used as a qualitative test for the presence of an -OH group?
back:
PCl<sub>5</sub> is added to the unknown liquid at room temperature.

The evolution of **steamy fumes** (HCl gas) confirms the presence of a **hydroxyl (-OH) group**.

front: What are the **conditions and reagents** for converting an alcohol to a bromoalkane?
back:
The alcohol is warmed with a mixture of **potassium bromide** (KBr) and **50% concentrated sulfuric acid**.

The KBr and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> first react to produce HBr, which then reacts with the alcohol to form the bromoalkane and water.

front:
**True or False?**

Shaking with concentrated hydrochloric acid at room temperature is a suitable method to chlorinate both primary and tertiary alcohols.
back:
**False.**

This method only works for **tertiary alcohols**. Primary and secondary alcohols do not react with HCl under these conditions. PCl<sub>5</sub> is required instead.

front: What are the **conditions and reagents** for converting an alcohol to an iodoalkane?
back:
The alcohol is heated under reflux with a mixture of **red phosphorus** and **iodine** (I<sub>2</sub>).

The red phosphorus and iodine react first to form PI<sub>3</sub>, which then reacts with the alcohol to produce the iodoalkane and H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>.

front: What reagent is used to **dehydrate** an alcohol to form an alkene?
back:
**Concentrated phosphoric acid** (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) is used as the dehydrating agent.

The alcohol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid, removing the -OH group and a hydrogen from an adjacent carbon to form a C=C double bond.

front: Why is **50% sulfuric acid** (not concentrated) used in the bromination of alcohols?
back:
Concentrated sulfuric acid would **oxidise** the bromide ions (Br<sup>-</sup>) to bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>), giving different and unwanted products.

Using 50% sulfuric acid prevents this oxidation while still generating sufficient HBr to react with the alcohol.

front: What are the oxidation products of **primary**, **secondary** and **tertiary** alcohols?
back:
Primary alcohols are oxidised first to **aldehydes** and then further to **carboxylic acids**.

Secondary alcohols are oxidised to **ketones** only. Tertiary alcohols are **not oxidised**.

front: Define **Fehling's solution**
back:
**Fehling's solution** is an alkaline solution containing copper(II) ions that acts as an oxidising agent.

When warmed with an aldehyde, the clear blue solution turns opaque due to the formation of a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide. Ketones give a negative result.

front: What **colour change** is observed when acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is used to oxidise an alcohol?
back:
The solution changes from **orange** to **green**.

The orange Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> ions are reduced to green Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions as they oxidise the alcohol.

front: Define **Tollens' reagent**
back:
**Tollens' reagent** is an aqueous alkaline solution of silver nitrate in excess ammonia (ammoniacal silver nitrate).

When warmed with an aldehyde, Ag<sup>+</sup> ions are reduced to silver atoms, forming a silver mirror on the inside of the test tube. Ketones give a negative result.

front: In distillation with addition, the aldehyde distils off immediately because it has a much **..........**  boiling point than the **..........**  reactant.
back: In distillation with addition, the aldehyde distils off immediately because it has a much **lower** boiling point than the **alcohol** reactant.

front: How do you obtain an **aldehyde** (not a carboxylic acid) from the oxidation of a primary alcohol?
back:
Use **distillation with addition**: the oxidising agent (acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) is heated while the alcohol is slowly added.

The aldehyde distils off as soon as it forms due to its lower boiling point, preventing further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.

front: How do you obtain a **carboxylic acid** from the full oxidation of a primary alcohol?
back:
Heat the alcohol under **reflux** with excess acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.

Refluxing keeps all products in the reaction mixture, allowing the aldehyde intermediate to be further oxidised to a carboxylic acid.

front:
**True or False?**

Fehling's solution gives a positive result (red precipitate) when warmed with a ketone.
back:
**False.**

**Ketones cannot be oxidised**, so they give a **negative result** with Fehling's solution. Only **aldehydes** produce the red copper(I) oxide precipitate.

front:
**True or False?**

Heating a secondary alcohol under reflux with excess acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> produces a ketone.
back:
True.

Secondary alcohols are oxidised to **ketones**. Unlike aldehydes, ketones cannot be further oxidised, so refluxing does not produce a different product.

front: Why must **acidified** potassium dichromate(VI) be used to oxidise alcohols rather than the dichromate solution alone?
back:
The reduction of dichromate ions requires **H****<sup>+</sup>**** ions** to proceed.

The acid (such as dilute sulfuric acid) provides these H<sup>+</sup> ions, allowing Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> to act as an effective oxidising agent.

front: What is the difference in purpose between **heating under reflux** and **distillation** in organic chemistry?
back:
Heating under reflux keeps all chemicals inside the reaction vessel to allow a reaction to proceed as fully as possible.

**Distillation** is used to separate a desired product from a mixture by exploiting differences in **boiling point**.

front: Define **molecular ion** in mass spectroscopy
back:
The **molecular ion** (M<sup>+</sup>) is formed when a molecule is bombarded with high-energy electrons and loses one electron, producing a positively charged ion with one unpaired electron.

The peak with the highest m/z value in a mass spectrum corresponds to the molecular ion and gives the molecular mass of the compound.

front: Define **infrared (IR) spectroscopy**
back:
**Infrared spectroscopy** is an analytical technique used to identify compounds based on the absorption of infrared radiation by bonds in a molecule.

When bonds absorb IR radiation at their resonance frequency, they vibrate by stretching, bending or twisting, and the absorbed frequencies are characteristic of specific functional groups.

front: Why is an **electric heating mantle** used instead of a Bunsen burner when distilling organic compounds?
back:
Electric heating mantles allow the temperature to be **controlled** more precisely.

They are also safer because organic compounds are often **flammable**, and an open Bunsen burner flame poses a fire or explosion risk.

front: Define **base peak** in a mass spectrum
back:
The **base peak** is the peak corresponding to the most abundant ion fragment in a mass spectrum.

It is the tallest peak in the spectrum and is given a relative abundance of 100%.

front: Define **wavenumber** in infrared spectroscopy
back:
**Wavenumber** (units: cm<sup>-1</sup>) is the reciprocal of the wavelength of infrared radiation.

It is used on the x-axis of an IR spectrum to show at which frequencies specific bonds absorb IR radiation.

front: A pure compound has a **sharp**, **..........**  boiling point. If impurities are present, the boiling point may appear **..........**  than the literature value or the sample may boil over a **..........**  of temperatures.
back: A pure compound has a **sharp**, **single** boiling point. If impurities are present, the boiling point may appear **higher** than the literature value or the sample may boil over a **range** of temperatures.

front: What causes the **[M+1] peak** in a mass spectrum?
back:
The [M+1] peak is caused by the natural abundance of the **carbon-13** isotope (just over 1%).

Molecules containing C-13 instead of C-12 have a mass one unit higher than the molecular ion. The larger the number of carbon atoms in the molecule, the taller the [M+1] peak.

front: What do the **width** and **intensity** of an IR absorption peak tell us about a bond?
back:
The width indicates whether the absorption is **broad** or **sharp**: for example, O-H bonds in alcohols absorb broadly due to hydrogen bonding.

The intensity indicates whether it is **strong** or **weak**: the C=O carbonyl group gives a strong, sharp absorption peak.

front:
**True or False?**

In a condenser, cooling water enters at the top and exits at the bottom.
back:
**False.**

Cooling water enters at the **bottom** of the condenser and exits at the top. This counter-current flow maximises cooling efficiency.

front: How is the **m/z ratio** calculated and which ions are deflected most in a mass spectrometer?
back:
The m/z ratio is calculated as the mass (m) of the ion divided by its charge (z).

Ions with a **small** m/z ratio (small mass or high positive charge) are deflected the most and are detected first.

front: Describe the characteristic IR absorption of the **O-H group** in an alcohol.
back:
The O-H group in an alcohol gives a **broad**, **strong** absorption in the region of approximately **3200-3500 cm**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

The broadness is due to the varying strengths of hydrogen bonds between alcohol molecules.

front: Describe how a **separating funnel** is used to isolate an organic product from an aqueous layer.
back:
The mixture is transferred to a **separating funnel** and inverted with the stopcock open to release pressure, repeating this several times.

The two layers are allowed to separate, then the lower **aqueous layer** is drained off through the stopcock and the **organic layer** is collected separately.

front: In a mass spectrum, the peak with the **..........**  m/z value corresponds to the **..........**  ion and gives the **..........**  of the compound.
back: In a mass spectrum, the peak with the **highest** m/z value corresponds to the **molecular** ion and gives the **molecular mass** of the compound.

front: Describe the characteristic IR absorption of the **C=O (carbonyl) group** in a ketone.
back:
The C=O group in a ketone gives a **strong**, **sharp** absorption at approximately **1710 cm**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

This peak is distinct and easily identified in an IR spectrum.

front: What is the purpose of using a **drying agent** in the purification of an organic product?
back:
A **drying agent** is an anhydrous inorganic salt used to remove trace amounts of **water** from an organic product.

Common drying agents include anhydrous calcium chloride (for hydrocarbons) and anhydrous calcium or magnesium sulfate (for general use).

front:
**True or False?**

The base peak in a mass spectrum is always the molecular ion peak.
back:
**False.**

The **base peak** is the most abundant ion, which is often a fragment rather than the molecular ion. The molecular ion peak has the highest m/z value but is not always the most abundant.

front: In IR spectroscopy, molecules absorb IR radiation at their **..........**  frequency, causing bonds to **..........**  by stretching, bending or twisting.
back: In IR spectroscopy, molecules absorb IR radiation at their **resonance** frequency, causing bonds to **vibrate** by stretching, bending or twisting.

front:
**True or False?**

If the drying agent clumps together, the organic product is dry and no more drying agent is needed.
back:
**False.**

Clumping means the drying agent has absorbed water and **water is still present** in the organic liquid. More drying agent must be added until some remains dispersed as a fine powder.

front: Why do **halogenoalkanes** show two peaks of similar height near the molecular ion in a mass spectrum?
back:
Halogens exist as **isotopes** with different masses (e.g. <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br in roughly equal natural abundance).

Each isotope produces a molecular ion with a different m/z value, resulting in two peaks of approximately equal height at M and M+2.

front:
**True or False?**

All organic molecules absorb infrared radiation.
back:
True.

All organic molecules absorb IR radiation. The specific frequencies absorbed depend on the **bonds** and **functional groups** present, which is what makes IR spectroscopy useful for identifying compounds.

front: An aldehyde distils off more easily than the primary alcohol used to make it because the aldehyde has a **..........**  boiling point, as it has lost the ability to form **..........**  bonds.
back: An aldehyde distils off more easily than the primary alcohol used to make it because the aldehyde has a **lower** boiling point, as it has lost the ability to form **hydrogen** bonds.

front: What **characteristic fragment peak** do alcohols typically show in mass spectra?
back:
Alcohols commonly show a peak at m/z = 31, corresponding to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup> fragment.

They also often show a peak **18 units below** the molecular ion peak, due to the loss of a water molecule.

front: Why should **IR spectroscopy** be used alongside **mass spectroscopy** to identify an unknown compound?
back:
Some IR absorption bands overlap each other, making it impossible to distinguish between certain functional groups from IR alone.

Mass spectroscopy provides **molecular mass** and **fragmentation** data that complement IR data to give a more complete structural identification.

front:
**True or False?**

Anti-bumping granules are added to prevent the reaction mixture from boiling.
back:
**False.**

Anti-bumping granules are added to **promote smooth boiling**. They provide nucleation sites for bubbles, preventing sudden violent boiling (bumping).

front: In the mass spectrum of propan-1-ol, the loss of a <sup>•</sup>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> radical gives a fragment with m/e = **..........**  corresponding to the ion **..........**<sup>+</sup>.
back: In the mass spectrum of propan-1-ol, the loss of a <sup>•</sup>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> radical gives a fragment with m/e = **31** corresponding to the ion **CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**OH**<sup>+</sup>.

front: How is an **unknown compound** identified using infrared spectroscopy?
back:
The IR spectrum of the unknown compound is compared with the IR spectra of **known compounds** in a database.

Absorption peaks at characteristic wavenumbers identify the functional groups present, allowing the compound to be identified.

front: How can you identify which layer is **organic** and which is **aqueous** in a separating funnel?
back:
Add a small amount of **water** to the separating funnel and observe which layer increases in volume.

The layer that increases is the **aqueous** layer.

front: Why is **fragmentation** useful when identifying an unknown compound by mass spectrometry?
back:
Different compounds may have the same molecular mass, so the molecular ion peak alone cannot distinguish between them.

**Fragmentation** produces characteristic peaks at specific m/z values that reveal structural information about the molecule.

front: What is a **gas syringe**?
back: A **gas syringe** is a piece of laboratory apparatus used to collect and measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction.

front: Define: **molar volume**
back: **Molar volume** is the volume occupied by one mole of a gas. At room temperature and pressure, the molar volume of any gas is approximately 24 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.

front: What are the two methods for collecting a gas produced in a reaction?
back:
1. Using a **gas syringe**
2. **Displacement of water**

front: What are the key steps in the method to measure the molar volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced from sodium carbonate and hydrochloric acid?
back:
1. Measure 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of **hydrochloric acid** into a conical flask
2. Add a known mass of **sodium carbonate**
3. Immediately connect the **gas syringe** delivery tube
4. Allow the reaction to go to completion
5. Record the volume of carbon dioxide produced
6. Repeat with different masses of sodium carbonate

front: To convert a volume from cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3</sup>, divide by **..........**
back: To convert a volume from cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3</sup>, divide by **1000**.

front: State three assumptions made in the molar volume experiment.
back:
1. Gas lost before connecting the delivery tube is **negligible**
2. The apparatus is **airtight** so no gas escapes
3. The reaction goes to **completion**

front: What is plotted on each axis of the mass-volume graph?
back: **Mass of sodium carbonate** is plotted on the x-axis and **volume of carbon dioxide** produced is plotted on the y-axis.

front:
**True or False?**

In the molar volume experiment, gas loss before the syringe is connected is assumed to be negligible.
back:
**True.**

The experiment assumes the amount of gas lost between adding sodium carbonate and connecting the delivery tube is **negligible**.

front: What is the formula used to calculate the **molar volume** of a gas from experimental data?
back: **Molar volume** = volume (dm<sup>3</sup>) ÷ moles. Read the volume from the graph, convert cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3</sup> (divide by 1000), then calculate moles from mass ÷ molar mass.

front: What safety precautions should be taken when handling moderately concentrated acids?
back: **Eye protection** and **gloves** should be worn, as moderately concentrated acids are corrosive.

front: State three assumptions made in a calorimetry experiment.
back:
1. The specific heat capacity of the solution equals that of **water** (4.18 J g<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>)
2. The density of the solution is **1 g cm**<sup>**-3**</sup>
3. **Heat losses** to the surroundings are negligible

front: What is **calorimetry**?
back: **Calorimetry** is a technique used to measure changes in enthalpy of chemical reactions.

front: What are the steps in the calorimetry method for a displacement reaction in solution?
back:
1. Place 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of **copper(II) sulfate** solution into a **polystyrene cup**
2. Weigh approximately 6 g of **zinc powder** (excess)
3. Record temperature every 30 seconds for 2.5 minutes
4. At 3 minutes, add the zinc powder (do not record temperature at this point)
5. Continue stirring and record temperature for a further 6 minutes

front: What is a **calorimeter**?
back: A **calorimeter** is a device used to measure heat transfer in a chemical reaction. It can be made from a polystyrene cup, vacuum flask or metal can.

front: What equation is used to calculate the **enthalpy change** (ΔH) per mole of limiting reagent?
back: **ΔH = q ÷ n**, where q is the energy transferred (in kJ) and n is the moles of the **limiting reagent**. A temperature increase indicates an exothermic reaction, giving a negative ΔH.

front: Define **specific heat capacity**
back: **Specific heat capacity** is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 K. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.

front: Why is a temperature correction graph used in calorimetry?
back: A **temperature correction graph** is used because some reactions are not instantaneous, causing heat loss to the surroundings before the maximum temperature is reached. Extrapolation gives the true maximum temperature change.

front: The equation for calculating energy transferred in a calorimeter is q = **..........**ΔT
back: The equation for calculating energy transferred in a calorimeter is q = **mc**ΔT.

front: State the three steps to construct a temperature correction graph.
back:
1. Record temperature before adding reactants for a few minutes to get a steady value
2. Add the second reactant and continue recording temperature and time
3. **Extrapolate** the cooling section of the graph back to the time of addition to find the true maximum temperature

front:
**True or False?**

In calorimetry calculations, the density of the solution is assumed to be 1 g cm<sup>-3</sup>.
back:
**True.**

This assumption means the mass of the solution in grams equals its volume in cm<sup>3</sup>, simplifying the **q = mcΔT** calculation.

front: State the key steps in performing a titration.
back:
1. Measure a known volume (20 or 25 cm<sup>3</sup>) of one solution using a **volumetric pipette** and place in a conical flask
2. Place the other solution in the **burette** (usually filled to 0.00 cm<sup>3</sup>)
3. Add a few drops of **indicator** to the conical flask
4. Open the burette tap gradually, adding solution portion by portion
5. Near the end point, add solution **dropwise** until one drop causes a colour change
6. Repeat until **concordant** results are obtained

front: What is a **burette**?
back: A **burette** is a piece of graduated glassware used to deliver precise, variable volumes of solution in a titration. It is usually marked to a precision of 0.10 cm<sup>3</sup>.

front: What is the **precision** and **uncertainty** of a burette reading?
back: A **burette** is marked to a precision of ±0.10 cm<sup>3</sup>. The uncertainty of a single reading is ±0.05 cm<sup>3</sup>, and the uncertainty of a titre (two readings) is ±0.10 cm<sup>3</sup>.

front:
**True or False?**

Concordant titration results must be within 0.10 cm<sup>3</sup> of each other.
back:
**True.**

Results are considered **concordant** if they are within 0.10 cm<sup>3</sup> of each other. Non-concordant results are discarded before averaging.

front: What is the **equivalence point** in a titration?
back: The **equivalence point** (also called the end point) is the point in a titration when the two solutions have reacted completely. It is shown by a colour change in the **indicator**.

front: Why is a white tile placed under the conical flask during a titration?
back: A **white tile** is placed under the conical flask to make the **colour change** of the indicator easier to see against a pale background.

front: The uncertainty of a titre is **..........** cm<sup>3</sup>, because two burette readings are made.
back: The uncertainty of a titre is **±0.10** cm<sup>3</sup>, because two burette readings are made.

front: What are **concordant results**?
back: **Concordant results** are titration results that are within 0.10 cm<sup>3</sup> of each other. Non-concordant results are discarded, and concordant results are averaged.

front:
**True or False?**

A burette is always filled to 0.00 cm<sup>3</sup> at the start of a titration.
back:
**False.**

The burette is **usually** filled to 0.00 cm<sup>3</sup> at the start of a titration, but this is not a strict requirement. Any starting volume can be used, provided both initial and final readings are recorded.

front: In a titration, 22.80 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> NaHCO<sub>3</sub> reacts with HCl in a 1:1 ratio. What is the concentration of the HCl?
back: Moles of NaHCO<sub>3</sub> = (22.80/1000) × 0.200 = 4.56 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol. Moles of HCl = 4.56 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol (1:1 ratio). **Concentration of HCl** = 4.56 × 10<sup>-3</sup> ÷ (25.0/1000) = **0.182 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>.

front: Name five pieces of apparatus used in volumetric analysis.
back:
1. **Beaker**
2. **Burette**
3. **Volumetric pipette**
4. **Conical flask**
5. **Volumetric flask**

front: What is **volumetric analysis**?
back: **Volumetric analysis** is a process that uses the volume and concentration of one chemical reactant to determine the concentration of an unknown solution. The most common technique is a **titration**.

front: Why is a three decimal place balance used when preparing a standard solution?
back: A three decimal place balance is used to measure mass as **precisely** as possible, reducing **measurement uncertainty** and ensuring the concentration of the standard solution is accurate.

front: What is a **standard solution**?
back: A **standard solution** is a solution of precisely known concentration. It is prepared as accurately as possible using a three decimal place balance and a volumetric flask.

front: State three ways in which concentration can be expressed.
back:
1. Moles per unit volume (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)
2. Mass per unit volume (g dm<sup>-3</sup>)
3. Parts per **million** (ppm)

front: What is a **volumetric flask**?
back: A **volumetric flask** is a piece of precise glassware used to prepare a solution of an exact, known volume and concentration.

front: The **concentration** of a solution is the amount of solute dissolved in a solvent to make **..........** of solution.
back: The **concentration** of a solution is the amount of solute dissolved in a solvent to make **1 dm**<sup>**3**</sup> of solution.

front: What mass of NaOH is required to prepare 250 cm<sup>3</sup> of a 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution?
back: Moles of NaOH = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol. Molar mass of NaOH = 40.00 g mol<sup>-1</sup>. **Mass = 0.0500 × 40.00 = 2.00 g**.

front: What is a **volumetric pipette**?
back: A **volumetric pipette** is a piece of precise glassware used to measure and transfer an exact, fixed volume of solution into a conical flask during a titration.

front:
**True or False?**

A concentrated solution contains a high concentration of solute, and a dilute solution contains a low concentration of solute.
back:
**True.**

**Concentrated** solutions have a high concentration of solute, while **dilute** solutions have a low concentration. These are comparative terms, not absolute values.

front: List the C-X bond enthalpies in order from highest to lowest.
back: C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I. The **stronger the C-X bond**, the slower the rate of hydrolysis.

front: What is **hydrolysis** of a halogenoalkane?
back: **Hydrolysis** is a reaction in which the C-X bond in a halogenoalkane is broken by a nucleophile (OH<sup>-</sup> or water), replacing the halogen with a hydroxyl group.

front: What reagent and conditions are used to hydrolyse a halogenoalkane in the laboratory?
back: **Aqueous sodium hydroxide (NaOH)** or potassium hydroxide (KOH) is used. The mixture is warmed, as the reaction is slow at room temperature.

front:
**True or False?**

Fluoroalkanes undergo hydrolysis faster than iodoalkanes.
back:
**False.**

**Fluoroalkanes** do not react at all because the C-F bond has the highest bond enthalpy of all C-X bonds. **Iodoalkanes** react the fastest.

front: How is acidified silver nitrate used to measure the rate of halogenoalkane hydrolysis?
back: Three test tubes in a 50°C water bath each contain ethanol and acidified **silver nitrate**. A different halogenoalkane is added to each, and the time for a **precipitate** to form is recorded. A shorter time indicates a faster rate of hydrolysis.

front:
**True or False?**

The yellow precipitate forms the fastest in the silver nitrate hydrolysis test.
back:
**True.**

The yellow precipitate is **silver iodide (AgI)**, formed from iodoalkanes. The C-I bond has the lowest **bond enthalpy**, making it the easiest to break.

front: State the precipitate colours formed when chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes are hydrolysed with silver nitrate.
back:
1. Chloroalkane: **white** precipitate (AgCl)
2. Bromoalkane: **cream** precipitate (AgBr)
3. Iodoalkane: **yellow** precipitate (AgI)

front: In the silver nitrate test, the **..........** precipitate forms the slowest because the C-Cl bond has the highest bond enthalpy.
back: In the silver nitrate test, the **white** precipitate forms the slowest because the C-Cl bond has the highest bond enthalpy.

front: Why is OH<sup>-</sup> a better nucleophile than water in halogenoalkane hydrolysis?
back: OH<sup>-</sup> carries a **full negative charge**, making it a stronger nucleophile than water, where the oxygen only carries a **partial negative charge** (δ-).

front: What are the key steps in the synthesis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane from 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
back:
1. Measure 8 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2-methylpropan-2-ol into a **separating funnel**
2. In a fume hood, add 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of **concentrated hydrochloric acid** in small portions, releasing pressure after each addition
3. Stand for 20 minutes in the fume hood, shaking every 2 minutes
4. Drain the lower aqueous layer
5. Add sodium hydrogen carbonate solution to remove acidic impurities, then drain the aqueous layer
6. Add **magnesium sulfate** to dry the organic layer, then distil and collect at 47–53°C

front: What is a **separating funnel**?
back: A **separating funnel** is a piece of apparatus used to separate two immiscible liquid layers, allowing the unwanted (aqueous) layer to be drained away from the organic product.

front: Why is sodium hydrogen carbonate solution added during the synthesis?
back: Sodium hydrogen carbonate solution is added to remove **acidic impurities** from the organic layer. It neutralises any remaining hydrochloric acid.

front: Why is magnesium sulfate added to the organic layer?
back: **Magnesium sulfate** is a drying agent added to remove traces of **water** from the organic layer. Once the liquid is clear, it is decanted and ready for distillation.

front: In this synthesis, **..........**cm<sup>3</sup> of 2-methylpropan-2-ol is mixed with 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of concentrated hydrochloric acid.
back: In this synthesis, **8** cm<sup>3</sup> of 2-methylpropan-2-ol is mixed with 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of concentrated hydrochloric acid.

front: What temperature range is used to collect the product by distillation?
back: The distillate is collected in the range of **47–53°C**, which corresponds to the boiling point of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

front:
**True or False?**

The fume hood window should be kept below the safety line to ensure the exhaust system works effectively.
back:
**True.**

If the window is raised above the **safety line**, the exhaust system cannot draw in fumes effectively, allowing toxic gases to escape into the laboratory.

front: Why must a fume hood be used in this synthesis?
back: **Concentrated hydrochloric acid** is very volatile and releases **hydrogen chloride gas** at room temperature, which is toxic. A fume hood prevents exposure to harmful fumes.

front: Why must pressure be released regularly when using the separating funnel?
back: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is volatile and produces **gas** inside the funnel. If pressure is not released by opening the stopper regularly, the funnel may become pressurised and could be forced open.

front: What are the two oxidation products of propan-1-ol?
back: Propan-1-ol is first oxidised to **propanal** (an aldehyde) and, on further oxidation, to **propanoic acid** (a carboxylic acid).

front: Why must an electric heater or water bath be used instead of a Bunsen burner in this experiment?
back: **Propan-1-ol** is flammable, so naked flames must be avoided. An electric heater or water bath provides controlled heat without the risk of igniting the alcohol vapour.

front: What is **reflux** in organic synthesis?
back: **Reflux** is a technique in which a reaction mixture is heated in a flask connected to a condenser, so that vapours condense and return to the flask. It allows prolonged heating without loss of volatile reactants.

front: What is the oxidising agent used to oxidise propan-1-ol?
back: **Acidified potassium dichromate(VI)**, K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq), is used as the oxidising agent.

front: Why are anti-bumping granules added to the flask?
